analysis.one_liner: Charges mining companies fees and royalties for taking hardrock minerals from federal land, and requires cleanup plans and bonds.
analysis.headline: The Senate passed it by voice vote in May 1993, but the House never voted on it, and Congress ended with no hardrock mining reform law.
analysis.plain_summary: Under an 1872 law, mining companies could stake claims on federal land and take gold, silver, and other hardrock minerals without paying any royalty, and could buy the land itself for as little as a few dollars per acre. This bill would charge a $25 fee to file a claim and $100 a year to keep it, add a 2% royalty on minerals from newly located claims, require fair market payment when companies patent federal land, and mandate cleanup plans, reclamation bonds, and quarterly inspections. It would also send one-third of the new money to mining states and create a grant program to clean up abandoned mines. It was the gentler of the reform bills circulating that year, written to avoid hurting the mining industry.
analysis.who_benefits: Federal and state taxpayers, who would collect new fees and royalties (two-thirds to the federal Treasury, one-third to the state where the claim sits); people living near streams and land poisoned by abandoned hardrock mines, who would benefit from a new federal reclamation grant program; and users of public lands, which would gain inspection, environmental-compliance, and cleanup requirements.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Taxpayers and communities near abandoned mines

how_it_helps.text: Creates a $25 location fee and a $100 annual maintenance fee per mining claim, with failure to pay treated as abandonment of the claim [S3].
Imposes a 2% royalty on the value of hardrock minerals produced from any claim located after enactment, with two-thirds of receipts going to the federal Treasury and one-third to the state [S3].
Requires companies receiving a patent (full ownership of the land) to pay fair market value for the surface of the land, instead of the nominal price allowed under the 1872 law [S3].

Requires Interior Department approval of operating plans for any mining that disturbs surface resources more than minimally, compliance with federal and state environmental laws, quarterly inspections, and fines of up to $2,000 per day for violations [S3].
Requires bonds or other financial guarantees covering the full estimated cost of reclamation before mining begins [S3].
Establishes an Abandoned Hardrock Mine Reclamation Program making grants to states to seal mine entries, control polluted mine drainage, and restore land damaged by past mining [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Hardrock mining companies operating on federal land: new filing and maintenance fees, a 2% royalty on newly located claims, fair market payment for patented land, reclamation bonds, and compliance costs. The bill was drafted to blunt these costs — every claim existing before enactment was grandfathered out of the royalty, holders of ten or fewer claims paid no maintenance fee at all, holders of up to 50 claims paid a reduced fee, and the Interior Secretary could lower the royalty whenever deemed necessary to promote development.
analysis.who_pays_short: Hardrock mining companies on federal land

drawbacks.text: The royalty applies only to claims located after the bill's enactment, so the vast majority of already-staked producing claims — including the big gold mines then seeking patents — would never pay it [S3].

The 2% royalty is measured at the 'mouth of the mine' and the Secretary may reduce it whenever necessary to promote development, making it far lower than what critics of the 1872 law were seeking [S3].

The bill's own findings declare that changes must not adversely affect mining employment, mineral supply, or the trade balance, signaling it was designed to avoid significant cost to the industry [S3].
Fees and compliance costs fall hardest on small claimholders, whom the bill partially shields through waivers and reduced fees for those holding fewer than 50 claims [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the public this was a genuine but modest gain: real money for the Treasury and states, cleanup money for abandoned mines, and basic environmental and reclamation rules on public land, at the cost of some burden on mining companies and possibly some mining jobs. Its biggest weaknesses are the grandfathering of existing claims and the low, adjustable royalty — it reformatted the 1872 giveaway more than it ended it. Compared with the tougher reform the House was writing at the same time, this was the industry-friendly version.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate passed it by voice vote in May 1993, but the House committee never reported it and no House vote ever happened; in November the Senate folded the bill into a broader mining measure, the two chambers' different reform versions were never reconciled, and the Congress ended with no law.

narrative.text: Sen. Larry Craig introduced the bill on April 5, 1993; it drew 14 cosponsors (12 Republicans, 2 Democrats) [S1][S4].
The Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee held hearings, ordered it reported favorably, and reported it without amendment on May 19, 1993, with additional views filed [S5].
The Senate passed the bill without amendment by voice vote on May 25, 1993 [S5].
The House referred it to the Natural Resources Committee and then, on July 6, 1993, to its Energy and Mineral Resources Subcommittee, where no further action was taken [S5].

On November 22, 1993, the Senate incorporated S. 775 into H.R. 322 as an amendment, and H.R. 322 passed the Senate [S5]. The House had passed its own, much tougher mining reform bill that year, with a higher royalty and limits on patenting public land; the two versions were never reconciled and no mining reform became law in the 103rd Congress (widely reported).

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Hardrock mining companies, which kept mining and patenting federal-land minerals with no royalty, no fair market payment for land, and no new reclamation or bonding requirements for existing claims.

sides.party_line_note: Senate support was bipartisan — a Republican sponsor, 14 cosponsors including 2 Democrats, and passage by voice vote — while the stall happened in the House, where a Democratic majority had its own, tougher reform bill.

industries.industry: Hardrock mining companies (gold, silver, copper and other metals on federal land)
industries.note: For the first time the bill would charge companies fees, a 2% royalty on newly located claims, fair market value for patented land, and reclamation bonds. But it preserves the 1872 claim-staking system outright, grandfathers every existing claim out of the royalty, sets a low rate, and lets the Interior Secretary cut it further to promote development — locking in cheap access to public minerals.

Holders of ten or fewer claims pay no annual maintenance fee at all, and holders of up to 50 claims pay a reduced $25 fee, keeping low-cost access to public minerals for small operators. The cost of that access continues to fall on the public treasury and public land.
States would receive one-third of all fees, royalties, and patent payments collected within their borders, giving mining states a direct revenue stake in extraction on federal land.
